§ 2Content

Poverty

  • Poverty is a state or condition in which an individual lacks the financial resources and essentials for a basic standard of living. It can have diverse environmental, legal, social, economic, and political causes and effects.

Types of Poverty

  1. 1. Absolute Poverty: A condition where individuals lack basic necessities like food, clean water, shelter, clothing, and healthcare, and education.
  2. 2. Relative Poverty: A condition where individuals have significantly lower income or resources compared to the average income level of their society.
  3. 3. Subjective Poverty: A condition based on personal perceptions of economic well-being, where individuals feel poor, despite their income level, influenced by societal comparisons, personal expectations, and psychological factors.

§ 3Poverty Estimation in India

  • In India, poverty is measured by checking a person's income or consumption level. If their income or spending is less than a set minimum amount, they are considered Below the Poverty Line (BPL).
  • Poverty estimation in India is carried out by NITI Aayog's task force through the calculation of the poverty line based on data captured by the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).

Pre-Independence Estimation

  • Dadabhai Naoroji through his book, "Poverty and Unbritish Rule in India" made the earliest estimation of poverty line (₹16 to ₹35 per capita per year).
  • He was the first person to give estimation of National Income of India.
  1. 1. National Planning Committee (1938)
  • It was set up by Subash Chandra Bose under the chairmanship of J L Nehru.
  • The National Planning Committee (NPC) of 1938 estimated the poverty line at ₹15 to ₹20 per capita per month.
  • This estimate was based on a minimum standard of living which implicitly included nutritional requirements.
  1. 2. The Bombay Plan (1944)
  • It was a set of proposals by influential business leaders in Bombay for the development of India.
  • Poverty line was suggested as: ₹75 per capita per year.

Post-Independence Estimation

  1. 1. VM Dandekar and N Rath (1971)
  • It was the first systematic assessment of poverty in India, based on National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data.
  • It was an Expenditure based Poverty line estimation.
  • It is adequate to provide 2250 calories per day in rural and urban areas.
  1. 2. Alagh Committee (1979)
  • The Planning Committee constituted Alagh Committee under the chairmanship of YK Alagh.
  • He constructed a poverty line for rural and urban areas on the basis of nutritional requirements and related consumption expenditure.
  • Rural: 2400 calories → Rs 49.09 per month
  • Urban: 2100 calories → Rs 56.64 per month
  1. 3. Lakdawala Committee (1993)
  • This committee defined the poverty line on the basis of household per capita consumption expenditure.
  • The committee used Consumer Price Index-Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) and CPI-AL (Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Laborers) for estimation of the poverty line.
  • It made few suggestions:
  • Consumption expenditure should be calculated based on calorie consumption as earlier.
  • State specific poverty lines should be constructed.
  1. 4. Tendulkar Committee (2005)
  • Tendulkar Committee was set up in 2005 to address the shortcomings of previous methods and submitted its report in 2009.
  • It computed poverty line based on Purchasing Power Parity in terms to ₹33 per day.
  • Recommendations:
  • It recommended to shift away from calorie based model and made poverty line broader.
  • Incorporation of private expenditure on health and education.
  • It replaced the uniform reference period (URP) with the mixed reference period (MRP) to estimate poverty in India.
  • According to Tendulkar Committee, the poverty line for 2011-12 was set to:
  • Rural: ₹816 per capita per month.
  • Urban: ₹1,000 per capita per month.
  1. 5. Rangarajan Committee (2012)
  • Rangarajan committee include three components in poverty baskets: food items, essential non-food items, and behaviorally determined non-food items.
  • In addition to calories intake it also include other nutrients like protein and fat.
  • It introduced Mixed Modified Reference period (consumption and expenditure was computed on weekly, monthly, and yearly basis).
  • The poverty line was recommended (reports submitted in 2014) as:
  • Rural: ₹972 per capita per month.
  • Urban: ₹1407 per capita per month.

Trends in Poverty Reduction

  • 2004-2005: 407 million people were poor (37.2% in BPL → Rural (41.8%) and Urban (25.7%)
  • 2011-2012: 270 million people were poor.
  • 1993-94 to 2004-2005: Poverty declined by 0.74% per year.
  • 2004-2005 to 2011-2012: Poverty declined by 2.4% per year.

State-wise Poverty (2011-2012)

  • Highest Poverty Rate: Chhattisgarh (39.9%), Jharkhand (37%), Bihar (33.7%).
  • Lowest Poverty Rate: Goa (5.09%), Kerala (7.1%).
According to Planning Commission, the % of people below poverty line is:
- Rural: 25.7%
- Urban: 13.7%
- Overall: 29% (2011-2012)

Types of Poor

  1. 1. Usually Poor: They are normally below Poverty line.
  2. 2. Churning Poor: They move in and out of poverty line.
  3. 3. Occasionally Poor: They are normally above poverty line.

§ 4Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)

  • The MPI concept was introduced in 2010 by United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).
  • It uses 10 Health indicators over 3 key dimensions, Education and Standard of living to determine the incidence and intensity of poverty experienced by a population.
  • NITI AAYOG launched a report in November 2021 → National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), that measures poverty in India using 12 indicators.

In recent scenario:

  • Multidimensional poverty in India has declined since 2005-2006 as measured by National MPI.
  • According to the NITI Aayog, 24.82 crore people have escaped multidimensional poverty in India in the last 9 years.
  • Uttar Pradesh: Largest number of people lifted out of poverty since 2005-2006.
  • Highest MPI (Most Poverty): Bihar.
  • Lowest MPI (Least Poverty): Kerala.

Head Count Ratio (HCR)

  • The head count ratio (HCR) is the percentage of a population that lives BPL. It's also known as the poverty headcount index.
  • Head Count Ratio = (No. of multidimensionally poor people) / Total population

§ 5Balance of Payment (BOP)

  • The Balance of Payment (BoP) is a record of all financial transactions (imports, exports, investments) between a country and the rest of the world over a specific period.
  • Types: Current Account and Capital Account.

Current Account

  • Current Account: This account scans all the incoming and outgoing of goods and services between countries. It is divided into:
  • Visible items: Exports and Imports of all physical goods such as tea and coffee. These are tangible in nature.
  • Invisible items: Exports and Imports of services such as shipping, banking, etc. They are intangible in nature.
  • Transfer Payments: These include unilateral transfers such as remittances, foreign aids, etc.
  • Top receiver of remittances globally: India.
  • 2nd: Mexico.

Capital Account

  • Capital Account: Capital transactions like purchase and sale of assets (non-financial) like lands and properties are monitored under this account.

Types of investment included

  • Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): It is a long-term investment in a foreign country's physical asset. E.g. Walmart acquiring Flipkart.
  • Foreign Institutional Investment/Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI): It is a short-term investment in a foreign country's financial assets. E.g. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, NRI deposits.
FDI limit in defence sector was enhanced in 2020:
- 74% through the Automatic.
- Up to 100% through the Government Route.

Current Account Deficit

  • A current account deficit is when a country imports more than it exports.
  • It includes the balance of trade, net income from abroad, foreign aid, and net current transfers.

Twin Deficit

  • A twin deficit occurs when a country has both a current account deficit and a fiscal deficit.

Balance of Payment Crisis (1991)

  • Balance of Payment (BoP) Crisis is also called currency crisis. It occurs when a nation is unable to pay for essential imports or repay its foreign debts.
  • India faced BOP in 1991 (then PM: P V Narasimha Rao and then Finance Minister: Manmohan Singh). In response to this, the government introduced broad range of reforms under LPG model.
  • L: Liberalisation → Abolition of industrial License Raj, reduction in import tariffs, etc.
  • P: Privatisation → The transfer of ownership or management of government-owned enterprises to private entities. It aims to improve efficiency, reduce the financial burden on the government, and increase competition in various sectors.
  • G: Globalisation → The process of increased economic, social, and cultural integration among countries through trade, investment, technology, and communication. It leads to the free flow of goods, services, capital, and labor across borders.

FOREX Exchange Reserves

  • Forex Exchange Reserves are assets held by nation's central banks or monetary authority holds to provide import cover and protect against external shocks.

The four main components of foreign exchange reserves are:

  • Foreign Currency Assets (FCA)
  • Gold reserves
  • Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) → also termed as Paper gold.
  • Reserve Tranche Position in the IMF (required quota to be maintained within the IMF → Higher the quota in IMF, higher is the voting power).
SDR Basket of Currency includes:
- USA
- Euro
- Yen (Japan)
- Yuan (China)
- Pound (Britain)

International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank

  • Headquarter: Washington D.C.
  • The Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 (officially known as United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference) was a gathering of 44 nations with 730 delegates which resulted in the creation of the IMF and World Bank (Twin Organisations).
  • It also resulted in creation of International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) which is now a part of World Bank.
1929-30: Great Depression in USA

Top Borrowers of IMF:

  • 1st: Argentina.
  • 2nd: Egypt.
  • 3rd: Ukraine.
  • 4th: Pakistan.
  • 5th: Ecuador.

NOSTRO and VOSTRO

NOSTRO

  • A Nostro ("our") account refers to a bank account that a domestic bank holds in a foreign bank in foreign currency → "Our account/money in your bank". It is used for international transactions and trade. E.g. Bank X has an account with Bank Y in Bank Y's home currency.

VOSTRO

  • A VOSTRO ("your") account refers to a bank account that a foreign bank holds in a domestic bank in the domestic currency → "Your account/money in our bank". It allows foreign banks to conduct transactions in the domestic market. E.g. City Banks partners with HDFC Bank based in India and opens an account with the denoted currency INR.

Certain Terms to Understand

  • Depreciation: A decrease in the value of the domestic currency due to market forces (supply and demand in the forex market). Exporters will benefit in case of depreciation.
  • Appreciation: An increase in the value of the domestic currency due to market forces. This happens when the demand for the domestic currency rises.
  • Both Depreciation and Appreciation occurs due to Floating Exchange Rate system (price of country's currency is determined by the market based on supply and demand).
  • Devaluation: A government-induced depreciation of the domestic currency under a fixed exchange rate system. Devaluation of currency will be more beneficial if prices of exports rise proportionately.
  • Revaluation: A government-induced appreciation of the domestic currency under a fixed exchange rate system.

Lorenz Curve

  • A Lorenz curve is a graph that shows how income or wealth is distributed within a population. It is used to measure inequality and to compare the distribution of income and wealth across different age groups.
  • (Graph 1: Lorenz Curve with axes "Cumulative share of people from lowest to highest incomes" (X) and "Cumulative share of income (or segment)" (Y), showing Line of equality vs Lorenz curve; Gini Coefficient 0 → 1, where 0: Perfect equality, 1: Perfect inequality)
Gini Coefficient or Gini Ratio can be associated with measurement of income inequality in an economy.
A fixed currency rate is often called pegged currency rate.

Exchange Rate Mechanisms

FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1973)

  • It was introduced with the intent to facilitate and simplify the foreign exchange system in India. This act was later abolished and replaced by FEMA since its rigid regulations were hindering India's economic growth.

FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999)

  • FEMA focuses on enhancing India's foreign exchange reserves and emphasises the promotion of foreign trade and payments.
